VulcanObservatory

A locally led water and community research programme, proposed for the Caldas volcanic plateau, Minas Gerais and São Paulo. Shared priorities, written protocols, local fellows and a community-facing report, with safeguards agreed before any fieldwork.

01The crew

A crew rooted in Brazil

Water, culture and coffee shape life across the Volcanic Alkaline Plateau of Caldas, Minas Gerais — and connect communities through water.

Earth Guardians Brazil grew out of a local fight. In 2012 residents of Águas da Prata (SP) learned a bauxite mine had been licensed at the edge of town; seven-year-old Tupã Levi joined the campaign alongside Levi Moisés. The crew was officially founded in January 2014 as one of the first outside the United States in the global Earth Guardians network. It works through campaigns, music, audiovisual production, school outreach and community digital tools. It holds Ponto de Cultura certification and an award from Brazil’s Federal Ministry of Culture (MinC).

2014Officially founded · Águas da Prata
~300,000People in the region
2 COPsUN climate conferences, recent year
02The context

A legacy site and a new rush

Community prioritiesThe proposed institute would support community-led monitoring of springs, rivers and riparian habitats on this plateau. Advocates describe some mineral waters as among the Americas’ most radioactive; the region also holds endemic biodiversity and internationally known thermal springs with longstanding medicinal bathing traditions.

Site history & reportingThe Osamu Utsumi mine, operated by Indústrias Nucleares do Brasil (INB) in Caldas, produced yellowcake from 1982 until 1995. The company’s own figures put peak acid drainage in the rainy season at 435 m³/h, and a 2009 thesis records 1.4 million m³ of treated acid effluent released into the Represa das Antas in 2001 alone. Local reporting cites more than 20,000 tonnes of stored radioactive residues and describes acid drainage at the pit and piles BF4/BF8, with leaching into nearby streams.

CALDASPLATEAU
RIO PARDODIRECT LINK
CACONDE → LIMOEIROPARDO CASCADE
RIO GRANDESAME RIVER SYSTEM

Connected watersheds need shared monitoring and evidence. The direct link is the Rio Pardo, which starts on the plateau and feeds the Caconde reservoir. Furnas lies on the Rio Grande upstream of where the Pardo joins it, so we do not claim plateau water flows into Furnas: it matters as the same river system and a landmark case of what dams do to riverside communities.

Open-air tailings & wildlife. Radiological risk is contested: the state agency says Caldeira residue samples are within tolerable limits, the companies cite nuclear-regulator assessments, and the MPF wants a conclusive ANSN opinion. We ask for open data and independent sampling, not for a verdict.

03The problem, continued

The rare-earth rush

Two projects are in licensing: Colossus (Viridis) in Poços de Caldas and Caldeira (Meteoric) in Caldas.

Poços de Caldas · Viridis

Colossus

Preliminary licence approved by Copam on 19 December 2025 after two postponed votes. Reported concerns: a mining area in the recharge zone of the Alkaline Aquifer, springs and headwaters in the project area (93 per the movement, 98 per federal prosecutors), and clay leaching of about 5 Mt a year. BNDES financing of R$ 77.5 million for a pilot centre was reported on 8 September 2026.

Caldas · Meteoric

Caldeira

Preliminary licence approved 19 December 2025; installation licence requested in March 2026 (reported value R$ 2.2 billion). Less than 2 km from INB’s decommissioning unit, with land purchases across ten-plus municipalities and a slurry pipeline that could demand very large volumes of water. Meteoric was reported acquired by Lynas on 30 September 2026.

MPF federalization requestFederalisation has not happened. Organisations from Caldas, Poços de Caldas, Andradas and Águas da Prata asked to move licensing to federal review. See “State of play” below for where it stands today.
→Community demands · Terra Viva / Água Rara

Agenda of demands

The volcanic plateau of southern Minas Gerais and eastern São Paulo asks not to become an environmental and human sacrifice zone.

Under the Precautionary Principle, the community asks to suspend ongoing licensing until a Commission of Mediation and Territorial Pact — coordinated by the Presidency’s General Secretariat, with federal bodies, civil society, public universities, municipalities and the companies — concludes a Term of Commitment and Territorial Safeguard.

12Demands
10 kmHydromineral & thermal protection
3 kmNuclear safety zone

Rare-earth mining banned in sensitive areas: a 3 km nuclear safety zone around INB’s decommissioning unit (Caldas); a 3 km buffer around the urban south-zone neighbourhoods of Poços de Caldas; a buffer around the Santuário Ecológico da Pedra Branca; and a 10 km hydromineral and thermal protection zone around known springs in Águas da Prata, Caldas and Poços de Caldas.

No use of existing public roads for raw ore, acid-leach pulp or tailings between pits, waste piles and the processing unit. Private internal roads only, inside the directly affected area.

No pipelines for raw ore or process effluents between pits, tailings and the processing unit, given the plateau’s geological and water vulnerability.

Send licensing from the Minas Gerais state agency to IBAMA; to ANSN for a binding opinion on radioactive materials; to INCRA, Fundação Palmares and the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples for prior consultation of Indigenous, quilombola and Roma communities (ILO 169); and to the CBH-GD6 river basin committee for a water-balance opinion.

A federally coordinated assessment of cumulative, synergistic and long-term impacts on aquifer recharge, water, soil and air, and on family farming, agro-industry, tourism and mineral-water bottling.

A technical visit with territory civil society and local university scientists to inspect consolidated ionic-clay rare-earth mines, assess historic liabilities and seek technology-transfer agreements.

Federal funding (BNDES, FINEP) for CITAR, the IFSULDEMINAS–UNIFAL-MG centre for independent lab reports and monitoring, and for the national seminar “Rara é a Vida” in Poços de Caldas.

No long-term pre-sale or streaming of mixed rare-earth carbonate (MREC) or raw concentrates abroad; priority supply for refining and industry in Brazil.

Export of rare earths only for civil, scientific and just energy-transition purposes, never for military technology, armaments or defence supply chains.

Seats with voice and vote for plateau civil society in the National Mining Policy Council, federal rare-earth working groups and the future governance body under Bill 2780.

A specific progressive CFEM rate for rare earths and a risk-compensation fund directed mainly to mined municipalities.

A CONAMA technical chamber to set strict national environmental standards for wet-leach rare-earth mining in ionic clays.

Earth Guardians Brazil timeline of action

2012

24 September: Xô Mineradoras is born in Águas da Prata after the Morro do Serrote bauxite licence becomes public. In December the municipality annuls the licences.

2013

The companies appeal and lose in every instance. The Organic Law is amended by popular initiative.

2014

In January Levi Moisés and Tupã Levi officially found Earth Guardians Brazil.

2015

“Protect Our Future”, Indigenous April with Wera Jeguaka, native crops planted at EMEB Áurea Soares. The School of Guardians begins.

2016/17

International partners; music and free agroecology workshops; reforestation. In 2017 SOS Águas da Prata gives the School a space and official status.

2018

Kit Amig@s da Água: youth-designed river pH, water quality and aquatic life kit, internationally funded.

2019

7K Project: reforestation and restoration of degraded areas, with water, flora and fauna monitoring.

2021/22

Khyentse Foundation Ashoka grant helps create the Bhumisparsha School (January 2022). CAN 2022 community field action.

2022/26

Public assemblies, Legislative Assembly work, and water and radioactivity films backed by the Ministry of Agrarian Development.

2025/26

Terra Viva / Água Rara, the federalisation request, the film Prata Ativa, and the federal delegation visit of 25–26 June.

→The volcano beneath · USP research

A collapsed caldera, 33 km wide

The Poços de Caldas Alkaline Massif is the largest alkaline complex in Brazil: a Late Cretaceous volcanic caldera whose semi-circular plateau stands up to 400 m above the surrounding flatlands. Original cerrado now lies mostly under pasture.

800 km²Alkaline massif
1300 mMean plateau altitude
1600 mHighest borders (1500–1600)
40°Steepest edge slopes

Nepheline syenites, phonolites and volcaniclastic rocks dominate. Inside, the landscape follows NE–SW and NW–SE structures; a NE–SW fault crosses the entire massif. Springs, streams and mines sit on this ancient, fractured ground.

The ground has a memory

Isobase analysis reveals where recent tectonics, not only rock type, shapes the plateau. Those faults are conduits: they carry mine seepage and tailings leakage straight into springs, streams and the Rio Pardo. Knowing this terrain is the first layer of knowing its water — and of defending it.

Ancient faults still move beneath the plateau. Every borehole, pit and waste pile sits on ground that remembers — and leaks.

Grohmann, Riccomini & Alves · Computers & Geosciences 33 (2007)

05Methodology

How we work

A locally led cycle that turns community knowledge into evidence people can use, trust and act on.

01

Co-design

Priorities, sites and questions set with local partners and affected communities.

02

Monitor

Fellows and community monitors observe springs, rivers, forests and protected areas.

03

Interpret

Data is collected, mapped and checked, then explained in plain language.

04

Share

Findings go first to the communities, then to press, schools and institutions.

05

Act

Evidence supports restoration, public assemblies and legal and policy requests.

05The wider circle

Who holds the mineral rights

Every ANM / SIGMINE mining process inside the 300 km zone of attention centred on INB Caldas (MG and SP files, 14 October 2026). A polygon is a right or application, not a licence.

8,960Processes in the zone
218Rare earths · all at research stage
243Other critical minerals
529Bauxite / aluminium
Largest rare-earth holders (ANM titular)

The five largest holders account for 111 of 218 processes (51%). 171 of the 218 were filed in 2023–24; only four before 2022. Registered polygon areas; corporate groups not yet mapped.

The pressure is concentrated. 127 of 218 rare-earth processes lie within 25 km of INB Caldas, so a modest network of sites can cover them.

Rights are layered. Rare earths, bauxite, potash, zirconium, lithium and uranium overlap, so we monitor for the water, not a single mineral.

Bauxite: the ghost of 2012. CBA and Curimbaba rights, whose licences Águas da Prata stopped, remain registered at ANM.

Baseline first. No rare-earth process has a mining concession yet, so evidence gathered now pre-dates any operation.

06One river system

Many waters, one system

From the plateau, the Rio Pardo runs through Caconde, Euclides da Cunha and Limoeiro to the Rio Grande. Furnas is on the Rio Grande itself.

The direct hydrological link is the Rio Pardo. We do not claim plateau water reaches Furnas; it matters as the same river system and as a place where decisions made far away shape local lives.
